stem:
Read the following passage carefully and answer the questions that follow.

Cities often respond to rising summer temperatures by planting trees. The intervention seems straightforward: more trees should mean more shade and cooler streets. Yet the number of saplings planted is a poor measure of the relief residents actually receive. Young trees may take years to cast substantial shade, and without adequate watering and maintenance many will not survive. Even mature trees can be concentrated in parks or affluent neighbourhoods, leaving crowded streets and bus stops exposed.

Measurements also shape what officials believe they have achieved. Satellite images can estimate tree cover or the temperature of surfaces, but these indicators are not identical to the heat people experience. A roof that reflects sunlight may register as cooler without making a nearby pavement comfortable for pedestrians. Conversely, a street’s temperature at one hour may fail to capture the exposure of people waiting there later in the day.

None of this makes measurement futile. It means that a single, easily counted indicator can conceal differences in survival, location and human exposure. A more useful assessment would track whether trees endure, where shade is created, and who benefits from it. Such measures may be slower and less tidy than a planting total, but they better connect municipal effort to the purpose that justifies it: reducing heat where people are most vulnerable.

Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Tree planting is an ineffective response to urban heat because young trees provide little immediate shade.
Satellite measurements are too unreliable to help officials evaluate neighbourhood environmental conditions.
Cities should assess tree-planting programmes through measures that reflect lasting shade and residents’ exposure.
Urban heat can be reduced most fairly by replacing parks with trees along busy streets.

verdicts.working: The passage argues that planting totals and surface measurements can mislead; assessment should track tree survival, shade location, and residents’ exposure.
